items.title: Poundland staff fear they’ll be left out in the cold for Christmas. When will workers have a say in their future? | Polly Toynbee

They are among 11,000 staff whose jobs are now at risk, but some shops might get bought by other chains. “Do you know,” Aboud asks me, “can we find out if this store might be saved?” I can’t, and the liquidators are only just starting work. He can no longer get through to his senior regional manager: “He doesn’t pick up now.”

items.title: ‘An epic fail’: Crypto world blasts Netflix’s ‘The Altruists’ for turning SBF’s crimes into a love story
items.summary:
A new Netflix series that tells the story of crypto crook Sam Bankman-Fried is winning decent reviews from TV critics and the public. But not everyone is a fan. People familiar with the crypto industry are taking to social media to blast the makers of “The Altruists” for distorting the nature of Bankman-Fried’s relationship with one-time girlfriend, Caroline Ellison, and for depicting the convicted felons as misguided idealists. The series, which dropped last week, is also taking fire for suggesting without evidence that Binance founder Changpeng Zhao is the real villain of the story—a depiction some claim is rooted in anti-Chinese racism.

The 8-part series, which lists Barack and Michelle Obama as executive producers, is based on real-world events that led to the 2022 collapse of Bankman-Fried’s crypto exchange, FTX. A subsequent FBI investigation resulted in Ellison pleading guilty and testifying against her former boyfriend, who is currently serving 25 years in federal prison for defrauding customers of billions of dollars.

Filmmakers regularly take liberties in order to increase dramatic impact. In the case of “The Altruists”, though, critics say the series engages in outright falsehoods by minimizing Bankman-Fried’s crimes, and depicting him as a victim who acted under duress from Binance’s Zhao. Don Wilson, the CEO of the crypto market-making firm DRW, posted a widely-shared clip from The Altruists showing Zhao and Bankman-Fried on X, describing it as “preposterous” and “an epic fail.”

This is an epic fail by Netflix. Recasting this as something @SBF_FTX and…
items.t: ‘An epic fail’: Crypto world blasts Netflix’s ‘The Altruists’ for turning SBF’s crimes into a love story

items.title: Global stocks move upward despite shock warning from Panmure Liberum analyst who sold all equities in his personal portfolio
items.summary:
With America offline for Thanksgiving, the rest of the world enjoyed a break from the market chaos caused by U.S. tariff policy, U.S. AI investment, and U.S. interest rate rises. 

In Asia, stocks broadly rose. Europe was up strongly. And although New York was closed for the holiday, S&P 500 futures were up.

Nasdaq 100 futures were up 0.63%, and Nvidia was up 1.29% in after-market trading.

None of this should be happening!

There is nothing but bad news on the horizon, multiple Wall Street and London City analysts said in emails to Fortune .

The most dramatic warning came from Panmure Liberum’s Joachim Klement (who writes a well-regarded Substack on investing whose subtitle is “Thoughts on financial markets by a grumpy, middle-aged German. What more do you want?”)

He gave a video talk in which he announced he was selling all the equities—all of them!—in his personal investment portfolio because of the recent selloff in the S&P 500: “I think that we are heading towards a major bear market with more than 30% drawdown risk.” His official forecast for 2027 is that the S&P 500 will sink to 5,000—a level that right now seems unthinkable. His concern is that the index is currently trading below its 200-day moving average: “As Paul Tudor Jones the famous investor once said, nothing good happens below the 200-day moving average.” 

“It doesn’t look like the Santa Claus rally is in store for us this year” 

Three factors are driving the gloom:

Firstly, inflation is still too high. The Fed’s preferred metric, the index for personal consumption expenditures, was up year-over-year…
items.t: Global stocks move upward despite shock warning from Panmure Liberum analyst who sold all equities in his personal portfolio

items.title: Reddit’s stock has taken a battering this year, but its COO says it’s barely started banking ‘over a decade of karma’ from devoted users
items.summary:
Reddit boasts engagement metrics that would be the envy of many other online platforms: Over 80% of its monetization comes from loyal, logged-in users, who spend eight times as much time on the site in their fifth year as they did in their first.

And yet, Reddit’s share price is down 62% for the year to date, as the platform grapples with an internet increasingly shaped by AI.

In its Q3 earnings call in October, Reddit’s CEO, Steve Huffman, said Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode were leading to a decline in search referrals to the site, the lifeblood of many social and media-adjacent businesses. The market did not like the implications, and the share price dropped from just shy of $130 apiece to a little under $91 overnight.

Chief Operating Officer Jen Wong told Fortune in an exclusive interview that some factors were lost in translation. The shifting relationship between Reddit and search engines “requires a different kind of partnership,” she said, rather than any separation. If anything, Wong believes Reddit is well-positioned to navigate the new era of online information gathering.

In their first year on Reddit, users tend to spend five minutes a day on the app or website. By their fifth year, that figure rises to 40 minutes, Wong tells Fortune . The number of “communities” (topic-focused discussion groups) that users are in jumps from 10 in the first year to more than 100 by their fifth.

“Reddit is really interesting because we have users who have over a decade of karma,” Wong said. “Reddit typically gets you as a young adult, and then you season over time in…
items.t: Reddit’s stock has taken a battering this year, but its COO says it’s barely started banking ‘over a decade of karma’ from devoted users

items.title: American Express is giving away $1.3 million in cash to British small business owners—with no strings attached

The $209 billion financial services giant is handing out £10,000 (about $13,000) grants to 100 independent U.K. businesses, in partnership with Be the Business, a U.K. organisation that helps small businesses boost their productivity.

“We know that even a relatively modest investment can make a meaningful difference,” Hannah Lewis, country manager at American Express U.K., said, while adding that founders can use the cash towards “revamping their premises, reaching more customers or bringing something new to their community.”

In turn, helping them grow could help their local communities too. According to the scheme, one of the main objectives is “to help small businesses contribute to vibrant destinations, active high streets and socially connected local communities.”

Amex’s own research found that 75% of British consumers believe small businesses positively impact their local communities, and around two-thirds would be more likely to shop with a business that employs local people.

But there’s a catch: the cash can’t go toward just anything, and 5% is held back until winners prove how they spent it.

Free money, but not for everyone: How to apply for Amex’s £10,000 Shop Small grant 

To apply, you’ll need to run an independent, for-profit business with a valid Company Registration Number, incorporated on or before Dec. 1, 2025.…

items.title: I’m an AI leader at a tech giant. Our industry has stopped taking safety seriously | Anonymous
items.summary:
We’re developing the most powerful tech in history – but trust, safeguarding and privacy are being sidelined in favour of huge profit

I’m a senior AI leader at one of the world’s biggest tech companies, and the products we put out into the world are increasingly being recklessly rushed, without proper consideration. The tech industry used to take safety and privacy seriously, but lately I have become worried by how rash we have become. In a sector that is obsessed with being first, ethical hesitation is now viewed as a luxury we can’t afford.

If you want to properly understand the actions of big tech, you have to look at the industry’s culture. It moves fast and there is a mindset of constant one-upmanship. Being first matters financially. But just as importantly, competition is believed to bring out the best in people.

The writer is an AI expert working in the tech industry. A version of this piece originally appeared with the Bureau of Investigative Journalism as part of its Secret Source series, a regular column featuring industry whistleblowers

items.title: DoorDash global food access head: Hunger doesn’t take a holiday. Putting food on the table will take all of us
items.summary:
Hunger gets harder to bear at the holidays, when everyone else seems to be gathering around a full table. With nearly 48 million Americans experiencing food insecurity in recent years, including 14 million children, millions of Americans will be facing a Thanksgiving table that has less on it. 

No single organization can close this gap. It will take food banks, businesses, neighbors and public leaders all showing up.

At a time when everything seems to cost more, putting food on the table has become harder than ever. Hunger exists in every county, and increasingly often among those who never expected to need food assistance before. More than eight in ten people surveyed by Feeding America identified rising costs as the primary driver of food insecurity. 

The pressure is building for those in need. Recent changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), the nation’s largest federal nutrition assistance program, have contributed to a significant decline in participation. According to the Food Research Action Center, approximately 5.5 million people have lost access to SNAP benefits since last year.

Food banks and pantries have always been the country’s backstop. But now, like everyone else in this economy, they are being asked to do more with less. Organizations are bracing demand rivalling or surpassing experienced during last fall’s government shutdown that created unprecedented disruption to SNAP. Some food banks are experiencing demand levels exceeding the COVID-19 pandemic.

Getting food to people can be just as challenging as securing it. Many of…
items.t: DoorDash global food access head: Hunger doesn’t take a holiday. Putting food on the table will take all of us

items.title: A Mark Cuban-backed AI startup is helping families turn Thanksgiving conversations with their elderly relatives into lasting memories
items.summary:
As 81.5 million Americans travel at least 50 miles from home for Thanksgiving, conversations around the dinner table could present a rare opportunity for people to learn more about their aging loved ones. A new class of AI startups wants to help them preserve those conversations forever.

Charlie Greene, the cofounder and CEO of Remento, first learned about the importance of recording memories when his father, Don Greene, died during the hijacking of United Airlines Flight 93 on 9/11.

A 10-year-old boy at the time of the terrorist attack, which resulted in his father’s plane crashing in Shanksville, Penn., the now 34-year-old Greene mostly has a collection of old home videos to remember him by. 

So when his mother Claudette, 74, was diagnosed with stage-three lung cancer, he quickly acted to record her memories. With the intention of conducting an oral history interview, Greene searched “questions to ask a parent,” which Google morbidly autocompleted with “before they die.” 

When he started asking her the questions like “How did you get to elementary school as a kid,” she lit up, surprised he was interested at all. 

“The thing that blew me away about that experience was how unmorbid it felt,” he said.

Claudette is in remission, but her battle with cancer still left Greene “unhealthily fixated” on the idea of how to best preserve loved ones’ memories. In October 2023, he launched Remento, which sends older “storytellers” a weekly text or email reminder prompting them to respond to photos or questions chosen in advance by their family members, such as, “What was the…

items.title: Amazon workers on food stamps have tripled despite its record revenue—and it’s just the latest evidence of the new economy of shrinking labor shares
items.summary:
The U.S. workforce has made the type of history it likely wishes it didn’t. Working Americans are taking home the smallest percentage of economic output , 52.8%, since the Bureau of Labor Statistics began tracking the metric in 1947.

But as the share of wealth workers take home through wages—called labor share—is shrinking, corporate profits have exploded , with the S&P 500 index gaining 600% since the beginning of the century, while wages have increased just 12.5% over the same period, adjusted for inflation.

In other words: Corporations are raking in cash, but American workers are reaping less and less of the rewards. 

The consequences associated with shrinking labor shares are now becoming tangible. A recent Government Accountability Office (GAO) report found that across the 11 states sampled, Amazon , the country’s largest company by revenue , has 12,346 workers on the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and 11,338 relying on Medicaid. That was nearly triple the number of Amazon employees in need of federal assistance compared to 2020, when GAO conducted a similar report. During that same period, Amazon saw an increase in annual profits from $11.6 billion to $77.7 billion. Amazon’s 2025 revenue soared 12% year over year, from $638 billion to a record $717 billion.

Amazon spokesperson Rachael Lighty told Fortune the conclusion drawn from the GAO report is “wrong,” and that it is misleading to look at raw numbers rather than percentages.

“When you look at the actual facts, you see that Amazon pay is among the best in the industry, regular full-time…
items.t: Amazon workers on food stamps have tripled despite its record revenue—and it’s just the latest evidence of the new economy of shrinking labor shares

items.title: U.S. Treasury has an unusual national debt headache: An $18 billion hole from GLP-1s, with families spending $500 less a year on groceries
items.summary:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent—and whoever comes after him at the end of Trump’s term—has an unusual new headache to consider when it comes to budget deficits. 

Investors are usually concerned with long-dated Treasuries pushing up interest rates, or international lenders choosing to put their cash into other assets. But in the era of GLP-1s, weight-loss medications are a new concern for the budget bottom line.

Nearly 60 million people will be using GLP-1s such as Ozempic and Mounjaro by 2030, Oxford Economics suggested in a note shared with Fortune this week. This is well above other estimates published earlier this year. JP Morgan predicted in February that 25 million Americans would be using the medication by the end of the decade, for instance.

But demand has surprised in 2026, so much so that Denmark’s national bank increased its economic growth estimates in September, largely due to U.S. demand for Novo Nordisk products Ozempic and Wegovy.

But with the drugs now covered by government health programs and contributing to potentially longer lifespans, Oxford Economics’ Grace Zwemmer writes that GLP-1s “are an additional factor driving a deterioration in the fiscal situation over the next decade.” 

Budget watchdogs like the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) have already said the fiscal impact of approving GLP-1s is going to be a problem for Medicare. In 2024, the CBO wrote that coverage of drugs for specific use cases would, on net, increase federal spending by about $35 billion between 2026 and 2034.

Zwemmer suggests the costs will be higher due to above-expected…
items.t: U.S. Treasury has an unusual national debt headache: An $18 billion hole from GLP-1s, with families spending $500 less a year on groceries

items.title: We may all be eating too much protein. But that won’t stop the influencers and big business | Devi Sridhar

Protein is the food industry’s current nutritional good guy. The fact that it’s often added to ultra-processed food makes it anything but

When I was growing up in the US in the 1980s and 90s, fat in foods was demonised. Low-fat yoghurt, low-fat desserts and low-fat margarine were all the rage, with the message that fat was bad for our hearts and arteries. By the early 2000s, concern had moved to added sugar and its apparent links to obesity and type 2 diabetes, driving food reformulations.

Sugar was replaced with artificial sweeteners such as aspartame and acesulfame K, which have their own health impacts. Aspartame is classified by the World Health Organization as possibly carcinogenic in humans, while observational research such as a 2022 study of about 102,000 adults has linked acesulfame K with increased cancer risk. Then carbohydrates came into the spotlight, with pasta, rice and bread becoming the bad guys for our diet and blamed for weight gain. There is a fashion cycle in nutrition, where each food group or ingredient takes its…

items.title: Why businesses are embracing ‘good enough’ open-weight AI—and how geopolitics could get in the way
items.summary:
As the performance gap between open-weight and closed-weight models narrows , a growing number of businesses—from local start-ups to large multinationals—are turning to open-weight models for greater control, customization and cost efficiency.

“ Frontier models at scale are incredibly expensive,” Damian Kim, the Asia-Pacific vice president of social media platform Pinterest , tells Fortune . “The cost to serve can be reduced dramatically when using an open-weight model versus a frontier model, where you’re at the whims of the API pricing.”

Anyone can download and customize the weights behind an open-weight model, which means firms can cut token costs while keeping tighter control of their data. They’re also taking a growing share of AI traffic. In August, open-weight models ran the majority of traffic on Vercel’s AI gateway; 56% of tokens routed through the cloud platform went to open-weight models , up from 7% last year.

“Models are converging on similar performance for industry use: U.S. government evaluators put the best Chinese model about eight months behind the American frontier,” says Olaf Groth, a professor of practice at UC Berkeley’s Haas School of Business. “For most enterprise workloads, that is good enough.” 

Rather than paying for the most powerful model for every task, companies are turning to cheaper, customizable alternatives for routine work. But with Chinese developers behind many of the leading open-weight models, geopolitics may matter as much as cost or performance.

items.title: The Guardian view on rising energy prices: only bold action can win public confidence | Editorial
items.summary:
Andy Burnham needs a radical vision of economic change to move on from policies aimed at giving voters ‘breathing space’

Ask Andy Burnham a question and it won’t be long before he mentions the cost of living. Responding to the results of midterm elections in the US earlier this month, he said that the Democratic party’s triumph meant that there was “an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living”.

This wasn’t a non sequitur. The Republicans lost control of Congress in large part because Donald Trump failed to address concerns about the cost of basic goods – a failing aggravated by the US president’s disastrous war against Iran, which caused a spike in commodity prices, exacerbating the affordability problem.

items.title: Sephora’s U.S. CEO initially turned down an entry-level job at the company because she could only wear black, white, or gray to the office
items.summary:
In 1998, Artemis Patrick turned down a job at a relatively small perfume brand that had just been acquired by the luxury giant LVMH. That company was Sephora, and 26 years later, she became its North America CEO. 

Patrick stepped into the top job for the global beauty retailer’s North America division in April 2024, earning a shoutout in its parent company’s half-year earnings call in July for “good performance.”

But Patrick’s journey to the top of the cosmetics empire started with a detour into cigarettes.

Patrick was studying for her MBA at San Francisco State University when a friend introduced her to the LVMH brand , which was hiring for entry-level planning roles. Patrick initially went in to interview for a role at the duty-free giant DFS in the only category that was hiring: tobacco. 

“I thought, oh my gosh, what am I going to be peddling cigarettes?” Patrick told the “How Leaders Lead” podcast in a recent episode. “This is crazy. So I [asked] if they had anything else, and she said, well there is this company called Sephora—LVMH just acquired it—and it sells fragrance.”

“Same salary, same building, because at the time Sephora was sharing the office floor with DFS. And I said, I mean, obviously I’ll take the beauty job. She said there’s only one catch: You have to wear black white, or gray.”

“And I said, I’ll take the cigarette job.”

items.t: Sephora’s U.S. CEO initially turned down an entry-level job at the company because she could only wear black, white, or gray to the office
